tier_reason: result.md compares against the vendored OpenSSL chacha-x86_64/poly1305-x86_64 assembly (pinned commit bee02b7d) and OpenSSL EVP, BoringSSL stitched AVX2 AEAD and Intel IPsec-MB, with raw per-run CSVs in results/raw; benchmark code is public (vendor/bench_aead_matrix.c, vendor/bench_raw_bands.c, vendor/bench_raw_chacha.c, report generator tools/report/result_report.py), the compiler (gcc) and flags (Makefile CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall, ASFLAGS -Wa,--noexecstack) are stated, and so are the CPU models (AMD EPYC 9655 Zen 5, AMD EPYC 4244P Zen 4). The gcc version is not stated, but the timed kernels are hand-written perlasm/NASM assembly.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page percentages are cycles/byte reductions, (theirs - ours)/theirs, not throughput ratios. Zen 5 AEAD real-world bands vs OpenSSL (vendored asm, called without EVP): seal +19.3% to +45.4% (WireGuard 1360-1420B +45.4%, i.e. 1.83x throughput derived from page data; 16384B +22.4%); open +20.9% to +47.6%. Zen 5 vs BoringSSL stitched AVX2: seal +49.4% to +57.1%, open +53.5% to +57.4%. Zen 5 vs Intel IPsec-MB (best of its two entry points): seal +3.8% to +16.8%, open +4.7% to +19.9%. Zen 4 AEAD vs OpenSSL: seal +8.9% to +33.0%, open +9.2% to +32.5%; vs BoringSSL +30.8% to +37.5%; vs Intel -1.3% to +8.9% (loses at Jumbo 8900-9000B). Raw AVX-512 ChaCha20: +25.0% to +33.1% vs the best other implementation (Intel) on Zen 5 for bands of 4KB and above (vs OpenSSL 16x about +29% to +35%, derived from page data); Zen 4 +5.0% to +7.6% vs best other (vs OpenSSL about +8% to +15%, derived from page data); ours loses to Intel at QUIC/WireGuard sizes (-7.5%/-3.9% Zen 5, -26.0%/-16.5% Zen 4). Raw AVX2 ChaCha20 vs best other (OpenSSL/BoringSSL): +10.0% to +10.8% on Zen 5 and +5.4% to +8.1% on Zen 4 for bands of 4KB and above; about 0% at 1200-1420B.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated; README requires Linux x86-64 with gcc and make), Makefile CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall for C harness/glue, ASFLAGS=-Wa,--noexecstack; kernels are perlasm-generated assembly assembled by gcc plus NASM (-f elf64) for poly1305_ifma.asm and the Intel vendor kernels
corrections.caveats: Single-author project with 1 GitHub star and no independent reproduction. Only two AMD CPUs tested (Zen 5 EPYC 9655, Zen 4 EPYC 4244P); no Intel CPU results. The AEAD 'OpenSSL' column is OpenSSL's vendored assembly called directly (no stitched AEAD in OpenSSL); OpenSSL EVP has higher fixed per-call cost (1419/1773 cycles vs 650/550 for asm). Ours is slower than OpenSSL asm on small messages (Zen 5 seal 64-256B: -19.6% to -24.0%; Zen 4 seal 64-256B: -9.5% to -23.4%) and roughly equal at exactly 1024B. Page flags power-of-two lengths (1024/2048/4096...) as flattering batch boundaries and uses realistic protocol-size bands for headline tables. Page GB/s figures assume a nominal 3.0 GHz; c/B is the real metric. Methodology is careful: perf_event_open core cycles, pinned core, alternating order, best of 7 x best of 3, round-trip correctness check before timing.

notes: Record's benchmark_url used /blob/main/ which returns 404; default branch is master, fixed. Record's 'seal +19.3% to +47.6%' merged seal and open ranges and its raw AVX-512 '+25-33% vs OpenSSL' is the README's figure, which on result.md is really vs the best other implementation (Intel); vs OpenSSL the margin is larger. License Apache-2.0, 1 star, last commit 2026-09-21, not fork, not archived: metadata confirmed.

tier_reason: README's 'OpenSSL comparison (make openssl)' block shows the claimed cycle counts, and the benchmark code is public (test/openssl_test.c, built by 'make openssl' with -O2), but the OpenSSL run names only the laptop (HP EliteBook 755 G5, Ubuntu 18.04.2, OpenSSL 1.1.1), not the CPU model or gcc version, so it falls short of A. The donna table has a CPU model (i7-2670QM) and compilers, but its baseline, curve25519-donna, is not OpenSSL.

corrections.baseline: OpenSSL 1.1.1 EVP_PKEY API: EVP_PKEY_ED25519 (CreateKeyPair, SignMessage via EVP_DigestSign) and EVP_PKEY_X25519 (CalculatePublicKey, CreateSharedKey via EVP_PKEY_derive)
corrections.workload: test/openssl_test.c: Ed25519 key-pair creation, X25519 public-key derivation, X25519 shared-secret computation and Ed25519 signing of a 32-byte message; min of 100 runs per operation timed with rdtsc (TSC ticks, minus rdtsc overhead), comparing the x86-64 assembly library build ('make asm && make openssl') against OpenSSL's EVP_PKEY API; outputs are memcmp-checked for equality
corrections.claimed_speedup: README OpenSSL comparison (HP EliteBook 755 G5, Ubuntu 18.04.2, OpenSSL 1.1.1; TSC cycles, the '@3.4GHz' usec figures are a fixed constant in the test code): CreateKeyPair 74,822 vs 210,738 cycles (ratio 2.817, delta 64.50%); CalculatePublicKey 316,096 vs 208,714 (ratio 0.660, Mehdi 51.45% slower); CreateSharedKey 270,930 vs 442,750 (ratio 1.634, delta 38.81%); SignMessage 78,628 vs 425,656 (ratio 5.414, delta 81.53%). The OpenSSL timed region also includes EVP_PKEY creation from the raw secret (plus peer-key and context setup for CreateSharedKey), while the Mehdi SignMessage call receives a precomputed 64-byte private+public key, so the CreateSharedKey and SignMessage margins are not like-for-like. Separately, X25519 base-point multiplication is 5.33x to 19.59x faster than curve25519-donna across the README platform/compiler table (README text says 6.2 to 19.5); fastest 43,229 cycles (W7-64/MASM V1.1, Intel Core i7-2670QM).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc via Rules.mk (version not stated for the OpenSSL run); source/asm64/Makefile compiles the C glue with -O2 -m64 -Wall -Wno-format -DUSE_ASM_LIB and assembles amd64.gnu/*.s with 'as --64'; test objects, including openssl_test.c, use -O2; RELEASE=1 adds -DNDEBUG, otherwise -g -D_DEBUG. The portable-C library (source/Makefile) also uses -O2. Donna table: VS2010/MASM, GNU assembler 2.25 (mingw) and gcc 4.5.3 (Cygwin-32).
corrections.hardware: OpenSSL comparison: HP EliteBook 755 G5 laptop, x86_64 (CPU model not stated), Ubuntu 18.04.2; donna comparison and internal cycle tables: Intel Core i7-2670QM
corrections.caveats: OpenSSL comparison dates from June 2019 (commit 'Performance comparison with OpenSSL') against OpenSSL 1.1.1 on one laptop whose CPU model is not given. OpenSSL-side timings include EVP_PKEY object creation from the raw secret inside the timed loop, and the Mehdi SignMessage side gets a precomputed public key, so the SignMessage and CreateSharedKey margins are inflated; the like-for-like CalculatePublicKey (X25519) row shows this library 51.45% slower than OpenSSL. Minimum of 100 TSC-timed runs, not core cycles. Current OpenSSL 3.x results are unknown. The curve25519-donna comparison (5.33x-19.59x) uses a different, non-list baseline across different compilers/platforms. Repo has had no commits since 2020-04-20.

notes: Downgraded A to C: the OpenSSL benchmark omits the CPU model and gcc version, and the record's claim that the portable-C build lacks -O2 is wrong (source/Makefile and source/asm64/Makefile both use -O2). Reading test/openssl_test.c shows OpenSSL timings include EVP_PKEY setup while the Mehdi sign path gets a precomputed key, so only CreateKeyPair (2.8x) is a clean win; X25519 public-key derivation is slower than OpenSSL. MIT license, 165 stars, last commit 2020-04-20 (abandoned), not fork, not archived: metadata confirmed.

tier_reason: PERFORMANCE.md compares ztls against OpenSSL 3.6.3 libssl (memory-BIO harness bench/bio.zig) and rustls (bench/rustls/src/main.rs), with the ztls harness in src/bench/record_protection.zig. Committed n=10 captures under docs/research/perf/ carry metadata: Zig 0.15.2 ReleaseFast with a native CPU target, and lscpu showing Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C (c7i.2xlarge) and Neoverse-V1/Graviton3 (c7g.2xlarge), plus an Apple M1 Max run. Code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated.

corrections.hardware: AWS c7i.2xlarge (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, x86_64, KVM guest); AWS c7g.2xlarge, which the page and README call Graviton4 but whose committed lscpu metadata shows Neoverse-V1 / 'AWS Graviton3 CPU @ 2.6GHz'; Apple M1 Max (macOS Darwin 24.6)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, native CPU target, crypto_backend=openssl (OpenSSL 3.6.3 libcrypto via nix); comparison backends OpenSSL 3.6.3 libssl and rustls 0.23.40 (x86_64) / 0.23.41 (aarch64, macOS) release profile, rustc 1.97.0 on the x86_64 capture; benchstat over --count 10 --benchtime 500ms. Captured at git revisions 2c102a5 (x86_64), e39f5a6 (aarch64) and 80083f5 (macOS), before ztls required Zig 0.16
corrections.claimed_speedup: Headline row (AppPingPong AES-128-GCM 1350B, x86_64 c7i.2xlarge, n=10): ztls 790.7 ns/op vs rustls 1447.5 ns/op (1.83x) vs OpenSSL libssl 1820.5 ns/op (2.30x). ztls executes 42.7% of libssl's cycles/op and 54.8% of rustls's on that row (row-perf capture). Faster than libssl on all 45 comparable app-data rows on x86_64, aarch64 and macOS (from +4% on ChaCha20 16384B ping-pong on aarch64 to +261% on AES-128-GCM 16B client-to-server on x86_64). Faster than rustls on all 30 AES-GCM rows per platform (x86_64 +65% to +131%). On x86_64 it loses to rustls on ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 16B/128B (-50% to -56%) and, per the benchstat file, by about 6% at 1350B (the page calls this an approximate tie).
corrections.caveats: Pre-alpha single-author project (7 stars) with no independent reproduction. ztls delegates AEAD, key exchange and SHA-2 to a libcrypto backend (OpenSSL 3.6.3 in all headline captures), the same library as the libssl baseline, so the win over libssl is TLS record-layer and wrapper overhead (WPACKET, tls13_cipher, BIO copies), not faster crypto. Only application-data rows over in-memory transport are compared; the handshake row is explicitly non-equivalent and not claimed. libssl gets one warm-up round while ztls and rustls do not. The captures used Zig 0.15.2 at older revisions, and current ztls requires Zig 0.16. The page labels the c7g.2xlarge host Graviton4, but its lscpu metadata says Graviton3 (Neoverse-V1).

notes: Numbers verified against docs/research/perf/20260712-102422-ec2-c7i-2xlarge/benchstat.txt plus the c7g and M1 Max benchstat files: libssl loses on all 45 comparable rows on each platform. The hardware field is corrected because the c7g host's own lscpu says Graviton3, not Graviton4. License Apache-2.0 with a vendored Zig MIT file (LICENSE-ZIG), both OSI; 7 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not fork, not archived.
